blocks.text: This lesson designs a data structure that supports three operations, each in average O(1) time: adding a value, removing a value, and returning a uniformly random value that is currently stored in the set. It is one of the most popular data structure design interview questions, because the natural first idea and the natural second idea each solve two of the three operations well and fail badly at the third.

The structure is usually called a Randomized Set, and the canonical version of this problem appears on LeetCode as Insert Delete GetRandom O(1). Solving it well requires recognizing that no single textbook structure, on its own, satisfies all three operations at once, and that the fix is to combine two structures so that each one covers the other structure's blind spot.

Before looking at any implementation, it helps to be precise about what each of the three operations must guarantee, since the exact return values and the exact complexity requirements are what make this problem interesting rather than trivial.

The core tension this lesson resolves: a hash set gives O(1) insert, remove, and contains, but has no way to fetch a uniformly random element in O(1). A plain array gives O(1) uniformly random access by index, but removing a value from it is O(n). The solution combines both structures so that neither weakness survives.
insert(val): adds val to the set only if it is not already present. Returns true if val was newly added, and false if val was already in the set (in which case nothing changes).
remove(val): removes val from the set only if it is currently present. Returns true if val was actually removed, and false if val was not found (in which case nothing changes).

getRandom(): returns a value chosen uniformly at random from the values currently stored in the set. Every element that is present must have an equal probability of being returned, and the set is assumed to be non empty whenever this is called.

All three operations are required to run in average O(1) time. It is this simultaneous requirement, insert, remove, and a uniformly random read, that rules out both of the obvious single structure solutions and forces a combined design.

content.title: 2. Why Neither a Hash Set Nor an Array Alone Works

blocks.text: The hash set approach
A hash set (unordered_set in C++) gives O(1) average insert, remove, and contains, because it hashes each value directly to a bucket. That handles two thirds of the interface for free.

The problem is getRandom(). There is no way to pick a uniformly random element out of a hash table in O(1). You cannot index into a hash set the way you index into an array, because a value's position inside the table is determined by its hash, not by any sequential order you control.

Even if you tried picking a random bucket instead of a random element, that still would not give a uniformly random element. Bucket occupancy is uneven by nature: some buckets are empty, some hold a single value, and some hold several colliding values chained together. Picking a bucket uniformly does not translate into picking an element uniformly, and scanning forward from a random bucket until you land on an occupied one, or walking a random distance into a chain, both introduce bias and, in the worst case, cost O(n) anyway.
The plain array approach

A plain dynamic array (vector in C++) is the mirror image. getRandom() is trivial and genuinely O(1): generate a random index in the valid range and return the element sitting at that index. Every slot in a contiguous array has an equal chance of being chosen, so the result is uniform by construction.

The problem this time is remove(val). An array does not know where a given value lives, so removing it by value first requires an O(n) linear scan to find it. Worse, once found, removing an element from the middle of the array and closing the gap requires shifting every element after it one position to the left, which is itself O(n).

blocks.text: Notice that the two structures fail at exactly opposite operations. The hash set is strong at insert and remove but blind to random access; the array is strong at random access but weak at removal. That symmetry is the clue: combine them so each one is only ever used for the operation it is good at.

content.title: 3. The Core Idea: Array Plus Hash Map

blocks.text: The standard O(1) design keeps two structures in sync at all times: a dynamic array that holds the actual values (in whatever order they end up in, not necessarily insertion order once removals start happening), and a hash map from value to that value's current index inside the array.

The array is what makes getRandom() O(1): pick a random index and read the array at that index directly. The map is what makes remove(val) O(1): instead of scanning the array to find where val lives, look it up in the map in O(1) and jump straight to it.

blocks.caption: The combined structure: the array stores the actual values, and every entry in the hash map points to that value's current index inside the array.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865495-370037698.png
blocks.alt: The Core Idea: Array Plus Hash Map

blocks.text: The two structures are two views of the same data, not two independent copies. Every mutating operation has to update both of them together, or they drift out of sync and the whole design breaks.

The invariant that must hold after every single insert or remove is: for every value v currently in the set, array[map[v]] equals v. Every operation below is really just "do whatever is needed to keep this invariant true."

Insert is the simple half. First check the map: if val is already a key in it, the value is already present, so return false and change nothing. Otherwise, append val to the end of the array, and record its new position, the last index of the array, as map[val]. Return true.

Appending to the end of a dynamic array is O(1) amortized. The array occasionally has to grow its underlying storage and copy existing elements over, but because that growth doubles the capacity each time, the cost of those occasional copies averages out to a constant amount of work per insert across many inserts.

content.title: 5. Remove in O(1): The Swap and Pop Trick

blocks.text: The map instantly tells us where val lives in the array, so the hard part of removal, finding it, is already solved. The remaining problem is that val could be sitting anywhere in the array, and removing an element from an arbitrary position normally forces every later element to shift left by one slot to close the gap. That shifting is exactly the O(n) cost this design is built to avoid.

The trick that avoids it entirely: instead of removing val from wherever it happens to sit, first swap it with the last element currently in the array. After the swap, val is sitting in the last slot, and whatever value used to be last is now sitting where val used to be. Update the map so that relocated value points at its new index. Then simply pop the last element off the array.

This works because removing from the end of a dynamic array is already O(1), no shifting is involved, the array just shrinks its reported size by one. By relocating the target to the end with a single O(1) swap first, an arbitrary position removal is turned into a last position removal, and the expensive shifting step never has to happen at all.

There is exactly one edge case to reason through: what if val is already the last element in the array? Then the index being removed and the last index are the same, and swapping an element with itself is well defined in C++ and simply leaves it unchanged. The subsequent map update reassigns val's own index to the value it already had, which is a harmless no op, and the following pop_back still removes the correct element. No special casing is actually required, the same code path handles it correctly.

items: Look up removeIndex = map[val]. If val is not a key in the map, return false immediately.
Read lastIndex, the index of the final element currently in the array.
Swap the array elements at removeIndex and lastIndex.
Update the map entry for whichever value just moved into removeIndex, pointing it at its new position.
Pop the last element off the array, this removes val, which is now sitting there.
Erase val's entry from the map, and return true.

blocks.caption: Removing 2 from the array 1, 2, 3: swap the target at index 1 with the last element at index 2 before touching anything else.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865495-931650934.png
blocks.alt: Remove in O1: The Swap and Pop Trick

blocks.caption: After the swap, popping the last element removes 2 in O(1), and the map is updated so the relocated value 3 now points at index 1.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406865495-573631184.png
blocks.alt: Remove in O1: The Swap and Pop Trick

blocks.text: With the array holding every currently present value contiguously, getRandom() only has to do one thing: generate a random index between 0 and the current size of the array, and return whatever value sits at that index.

This is uniform by construction. Every element occupies exactly one slot in the array, there are no gaps and no duplicated slots after a removal, so a uniformly random index over the valid range picks each stored value with exactly equal probability.

rand() % n is what most interview solutions use, but it technically introduces a very small bias when n does not divide evenly into the range of rand(). A production quality implementation seeds a proper generator once, for example mt19937, and draws from it with a distribution bounded between 0 and the last valid index instead. Interviewers are usually fine with the simpler rand() % n as long as you can name this tradeoff.
Start from an empty set and run insert(1), insert(2), insert(3) in order. Each one appends to the array and records its index in the map.

Now call remove(2). The map says 2 lives at index 1. The last index is 2, and the value sitting there is 3. Swap the elements at index 1 and index 2, update the map entry for 3 (the value that just moved), then pop the last element off the array and erase 2 from the map.

codes.javascript:
remove(2):
  removeIndex = idx[2] = 1
  lastIndex   = vals.size() - 1 = 2

  swap(vals[1], vals[2])        ->  vals = [1, 3, 2]
  idx[vals[1]] = idx[3] = 1     ->  idx  = {1: 0, 2: 1, 3: 1}

  vals.pop_back()               ->  vals = [1, 3]
  idx.erase(2)                  ->  idx  = {1: 0, 3: 1}

blocks.text: The set now contains exactly 1 and 3, correctly, with no leftover gaps and no stale map entries. Calling getRandom() generates a random index in the range covering the two current slots and returns whichever of 1 or 3 sits there, each with equal probability, a fifty percent chance for each value.

blocks.text: Putting the three operations together into a single class, using a vector<int> for the values and an unordered_map<int, int> from value to current index:

The constructor seeds the random generator once, which matters: seeding inside getRandom() itself would reset the sequence on every call and badly skew the results. The remove function deliberately does not special case the last element, the unconditional swap already behaves correctly in that situation, which is a good detail to point out out loud in an interview to show the edge case was actually considered rather than missed.

insert and remove are both O(1) on average, because each one does a constant amount of array work plus a constant amount of hash map work, and hash map operations are O(1) on average. getRandom is O(1) in the worst case, always, since it never touches the hash map at all, it is purely array indexing plus a random number draw.

That distinction between average and worst case matters. A hash map's O(1) is an average over typical inputs; under a pathological set of keys that all collide into the same bucket, a single hash map operation can degrade toward O(n). The array driven getRandom has no such escape hatch, it is genuinely O(1) no matter what values are stored.

blocks.text: A well known, meaningfully harder follow up is Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) Duplicates allowed, where the same value can be stored multiple times and getRandom() must still return each stored occurrence with equal probability, not each distinct value.

The array still holds every stored occurrence, duplicates included, so getRandom() needs no change at all: a uniformly random index over the array naturally returns a repeated value more often, in exact proportion to how many times it occurs. That built in weighting is actually the elegant part of this variant.

What has to change is the map. A single index per value is no longer enough, since a repeated value now lives at several different positions in the array simultaneously. The map becomes a value to a set of indices, typically unordered_map<int, unordered_set<int>>, so every occurrence of a value can be tracked independently.

codes.javascript: unordered_map<int, unordered_set<int>> idx;   // value -> all indices where it occurs

blocks.text: Insert now always succeeds (there is no notion of "already present" blocking a new occurrence), it appends to the array and adds the new index into that value's index set, returning true only the first time the value ever appears, exactly matching the base problem's semantics for a brand new value. Remove picks any one index out of the target value's index set (which one does not matter, since they are interchangeable), performs the same swap with the last element and pop, and then carefully updates the index sets for both the value being removed and the value that got relocated by the swap, since either or both sets may need an entry added or removed.

This variant is a strong interview signal question. A candidate who only memorized the base solution tends to get stuck, while a candidate who actually understood the invariant, every value maps to exactly where it lives in the array, generalizes it to a set of positions almost immediately.

content.title: 10. Common Mistakes, Problem Patterns and Interview Checklist

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to update the map entry for the element that got swapped into the removed slot. This leaves the map pointing at a stale index for that value, so the next operation on it silently touches the wrong array slot.

Assuming the last element removal case needs a special branch. Swapping an element with itself is well defined in C++, the plain unconditional code already handles it, but failing to reason through this case out loud in an interview reads as an unexamined edge case.
Calling rand() without seeding it once, which produces the exact same sequence of getRandom() results on every run of the program.
Calling getRandom() on an empty set, or computing rand() % vals.size() when size is zero, which is undefined behavior.
Checking membership with array[map[val]] == val style logic instead of map.count(val), which can insert a spurious default entry into the map as a side effect.
In the duplicates allowed variant, keeping a single index per value instead of a set of indices, which silently drops all but one occurrence of a repeated value from the map.

blocks.text: Problem patterns

items: Easy Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) (LC 380): the canonical version, exactly the array plus hash map design covered in this lesson.
Hard Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) Duplicates allowed (LC 381): the same core idea, with the map upgraded to store a set of indices per value.
Related Random Pick Index (LC 398): given repeated values, uniformly sample one index that matches a target value, often solved with reservoir sampling.
Related Random Pick with Weight (LC 528): a weighted variant, solved with prefix sums plus binary search instead of uniform index selection.
Related LRU Cache (LC 146): another "combine two structures" design problem, pairing a hash map with a doubly linked list instead of a hash map with an array.

blocks.text: Interview checklist

items: Can you state precisely why a hash set alone cannot support O(1) uniformly random access?
Can you state precisely why a plain array alone cannot support O(1) removal by value?
Can you implement insert, remove, and getRandom from scratch in under five minutes?
Can you explain in one sentence why swapping the target with the last element before popping keeps removal O(1)?
Have you reasoned through what happens when the element being removed is already the last element in the array?
Can you describe how the design changes for the duplicates allowed follow up, and why getRandom needs no change at all?

blocks.text: Once these questions all have confident, precise answers, this design is genuinely internalized rather than memorized, which is exactly what separates a smooth interview walkthrough from a shaky one.
